newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Labour Office less gloomy on jobs outlook.
newsitem.headline: German Labour Office less gloomy on jobs outlook.

text.p: The German Labour Office appeared less gloomy on Thursday in its view of how the labour market would continue to develop this year as German unemployment hovers at its highest levels since the 1930s.

The main difficulties remain in the building sector, where structural problems have driven the industry into recession, but the first rays of light are beginning to appear in the broader manufacturing industry.

The labour office seems more certain now that the trend in unemployment could begin to turn around by the middle of the year, improving Germany's chances of meeting the strict fiscal criteria to qualify for Europe's planned single currency.
"The government's forecast of 4.2 million average jobless in 1997 is not unrealistic," Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda told a news conference in Nuremberg.

He was speaking after release of February jobless data, which show unemployment rose 5,000 from January to 4.316 million on a seasonally adjusted basis. On an unadjusted basis, the unemployment rate was 12.2 percent with 4.672 million out of work.

"In non-construction related manufacturing areas, the rise in unemployment was noticeably smaller than overall. This could mean that the worst is over in job losses in the manufacturing industry," said Jagoda.
But the German economy still remains weak and provided no new stimulus for job creation in February.
While saying it was still too soon to make a reliable forecast for the full year, Jagoda added that he expected the jobless total to fall in March.

Hans-Peter Leikeb, head of the labour office's jobs market research wing, told Reuters after the news conference that new jobs could come from export-related sectors and a small rise in private consumption.

"Based on the forecast of 2.5 percent economic growth in the government's annual economic report I believe we will see a fall in the seasonally adjusted unemployment jobless figure at the middle of the year," said Leikeb.
"In 1997 the construction sector will not be a source of hope as there are long-term structural changes being made," he added.
